clinicalPearls: Caused by de novo truncating variants in ASXL1, a member of the polycomb group of chromatin regulators that partners with the deubiquitinase BAP1 in the PR-DUB complex and modulates polycomb-mediated gene silencing
The characteristic BOS posture consists of flexion at the elbows and wrists with ulnar deviation and fixed flexion of the fingers, often noted from birth
Trigonocephaly with a prominent metopic ridge, microcephaly, marked intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction and severe feeding difficulties are typical
A glabellar and eyelid naevus flammeus, prominent eyes, hypertrichosis and a characteristic facial appearance aid clinical recognition
There is an increased risk of Wilms tumour, so renal (nephroblastoma) surveillance with regular abdominal ultrasound is recommended in childhood
Feeding is frequently complicated by severe reflux, aspiration and apnoea, contributing to significant early morbidity and mortality
Diagnosis is confirmed by finding a de novo loss-of-function ASXL1 variant, and somatic ASXL1 changes seen in myeloid malignancy should not be confused with the germline disorder
reference.pathophysiology: ASXL1 encodes a chromatin-associated protein of the polycomb group that helps direct histone modifications governing gene repression, in part through the PR-DUB complex which removes ubiquitin from histone H2A and thereby balances polycomb silencing. Constitutional truncating variants disturb this epigenetic regulation during development, deranging the coordinated switching on and off of genes that pattern the skull, limbs and brain. The resulting misregulation produces the distinctive posture, craniofacial features, growth restriction and severe neurodevelopmental impairment, while loss of appropriate silencing at growth- and proliferation-related loci is thought to underlie the predisposition to Wilms tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic causes of trigonocephaly with severe developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to detect de novo truncating ASXL1 variants
Regular abdominal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour through early childhood
Assessment of feeding and swallowing, with consideration of gastrostomy for safe nutrition
Brain MRI to define structural anomalies
Sleep and respiratory evaluation for apnoea and airway compromise
Ophthalmological review for the ocular manifestations
Growth monitoring with attention to failure to thrive
redFlags: Cyclical vomiting, severe reflux or apnoea with cyanotic episodes in infancy
An abdominal mass or haematuria raising concern for Wilms tumour
Feeding intolerance with progressive failure to thrive
Unexplained apnoea contributing to sudden deterioration
reference.prognosis: Early mortality is substantial, largely from feeding-related aspiration, apnoea and respiratory complications in infancy; survivors have severe intellectual disability and require intensive multidisciplinary support, and lifelong vigilance for Wilms tumour is important during the years of greatest risk.
pitfalls: Confusing the germline syndrome with the somatic ASXL1 variants found in acquired myeloid disease
Omitting Wilms tumour surveillance and thereby missing an early, treatable renal malignancy
Underestimating the severity of feeding and respiratory problems that drive early morbidity
Mistaking the disorder for the clinically overlapping but distinct Bainbridge-Ropers (ASXL3) syndrome
references: Nature Reviews — polycomb chromatin regulators in development and disease
